processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: System modified to synthesize five different alloys in one operation for each alloy system; five Cu molds moved stepwise inside the furnace and were successively filled from a 4-kg ingot; after each cast the remaining melt composition was adjusted by charging Al through an air lock.
10 × 50 × 130 mm³-sized blocks hot rolled into 2 ± 0.1 mm thick and ~500 mm long sheets.
Sheets cut perpendicular to the rolling direction into sets of nine segments with dimensions 2 × 60 × 55 mm³ for each alloy composition.
This is the sample-defining step: after homogenization, aged in air at 600 °C for 24 h, then oil quenched.
Scales removed from the surfaces by low-pressure, fine-grit sandblasting after the heat treatments.
Samples for mechanical testing and microstructure investigation were prepared from the segments by package spark erosion.

structures.overall_structure: Fully recrystallized microstructure with a grain size of ~20 µm and some retained microsegregations of Mn (after hot rolling and water quenching).

Aged (600 °C, 24 h) Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl condition: austenite matrix with ferrite content increasing with Al; κ-carbide develops at 600 °C in the highest-Al alloy; ε-martensite also detected by XRD in some conditions.

precipitates.type: κ-carbide (j-carbide), L'1₂ ordered fcc perovskite-type carbide, approximate stoichiometry (Fe,Mn)₃AlC
precipitates.distribution: develops at 600 °C in the highest-Al Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl alloy.
precipitates.coherency: cuboidal nanoprecipitates in austenitic matrix (lattice mismatch below 3%); semicoherent with lattice mismatch as large as -6% in ferritic matrix.

phase_interfaces.coherence: lattice mismatch below 3% with respect to austenitic Fe-Mn-C matrix; can form cuboidal nanoprecipitates.
semicoherent; lattice mismatch as large as -6%.

interfaces.slip_behavior: After aging at 500–600 °C, twinning is reduced and strain hardening is essentially associated with κ-carbide (j-carbide) and solid-solution strengthening.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Increasing Al content promotes the formation of κ-carbides and ferrite; for this Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl class, increasing ferrite content is more relevant for the mechanical trend than κ-carbides or ε-martensite.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: Tensile specimens prepared from segments (2 × 60 × 55 mm³) by package spark erosion; cross-sectional areas of selected samples prepared in the plane perpendicular to the rolling direction.
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: All plotted values represent averages of three measurements for every material state.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: performed on the rolling plane of samples ground to a thickness of 1 mm.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Increasing ferrite content with increasing Al; the highest-Al Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl alloy develops κ carbide at 600 °C; ε-martensite also detected; increasing ferrite content is more relevant for the mechanical trend than κ-carbides or ε-martensite.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature; initial strain rate 10^-3 s^-1; averages of three measurements for every material state.
characterization_methods.purpose: mechanical property screening (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, total elongation)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl class, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength both increase while tensile elongation drops with Al content (2–11 wt.% Al).

characterization_methods.purpose: hardness screening as a function of Al content and aging condition
characterization_methods.key_findings: Hardness (HBW) has a minimum ~120–140 at ~2 wt.% Al and reaches ~290 at ~10.5 wt.% Al for the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl set.

characterization_methods.purpose: inspection for cracks/pores/macrosegregations and characterization of as-cast and recrystallized microstructures
characterization_methods.key_findings: No cracks, pores, or macrosegregations in the final materials; as-cast samples had a coarse dendritic microstructure; hot rolling and water quenching gave a fully recrystallized microstructure with ~20 µm grain size and some retained Mn microsegregations.

unmapped_findings: For the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl TWIP steels (second RAP alloy class), yield strength and ultimate tensile strength both increase while tensile elongation drops as a function of Al content in the range 2–11 wt.% Al (b0026).

XRD screening of the corresponding Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl samples indicates that the increasing ferrite content is more relevant for the observed mechanical trend than the presence of κ-carbides (j-carbides) or ε-martensite (b0026).

Fig. 6a (600 °C, 24 h is one of the four plotted conditions, red series) shows for the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl set: yield strength ~350 MPa at 0 Al, dipping near 2 Al, then rising steeply to the highest values (~690 MPa for the 500 °C condition) at ~10.5 wt.% Al; UTS starts ~810–840 MPa, passes a minimum near 5 wt.% Al (~550–580 MPa) and climbs to ~900 MPa (500 °C condition) at ~10.5 wt.% Al; tensile elongation peaks at ~80–85% at 2 wt.% Al and collapses to ~12–25% at ~10.5 wt.% Al; hardness (HBW) has a minimum ~120–140 at 2 wt.% Al and reaches ~290 at ~10.5 wt.% Al (figure_006).

Fig. 6b XRD phase fractions: the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-2Al alloy stays ~100 vol.% γ (with a small ε-martensite cap); higher-Al alloys show increasing α ferrite, and the highest-Al alloy develops κ carbide at 600 °C (figure_006).
Summary statement: increasing the Al content promotes the formation of κ-carbides (j-carbides) and ferrite in the Fe-Mn-Al-C system (b0109).
